newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Grains-Mouldy soymeal worry for China buyers.
newsitem.headline: China Grains-Mouldy soymeal worry for China buyers.

text.p: Some of the massive tonnages of soybean meal at Chinese ports awaiting buyers was rotting, leading Chinese buyers to demand even lower prices as meal quality deteriorated, some meal traders in China said Thursday.
"I've heard Chinese offers as low as 2,400-2,500 yuan ($289-301) per tonne for meal at (southern) ports," said a Beijing-based trader.
One trader said he had heard an offer as low as 2,300 yuan per tonne, with the Chinese buyer citing the meal's degenerating quality as a major factor.
The price of meal at ports was at about 2,700 yuan per tonne last week.
"It's warm in the mornings and cold at night, this affects the moisture content of meal and is a very serious quality problem," one China-based trader said.
Traders in China said that based on phone calls to various ports, they estimated the total amount of meal in storage at Chinese ports was between 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes.
Two small vessels of Indian meal, most likely 10,000-12,000 tonnes each, were heard arriving soon in the southern ports of Guangzhou and Nantong.
But the domestic price of meal might edge up, some traders said, since very few cargoes were expected to arrive in February and March.
In January, arrivals from South America alone were estimated at 100,000-200,000 by a senior trader in China.
Chicago Board of Trade soymeal futures closed higher on Wednesday, with soymeal $1.50 to $3.50 per tonne higher. March rose $3.50 to $240.40.

No meal was being offered for spot markets, and only South American meal was being quoted for forward delivery in late March or April, when the U.S. meal would no longer be available, industry sources said.
No Chinese enquiries were heard for soybeans and the market was said to be very quiet.
But some sources said Chinese traders expected soybean prices to go up in the spring and summer as domestic production had not been stellar.
The domestic price of beans still hovered at 3,000-3,100 yuan per tonne, with the bean price drop not as noticeable as corn or meal, traders said.
